# Unpacking the "Auth guard [] is not defined" Error in Laravel

When you register a new Laravel application and attempt to follow an older tutorial to set up authentication, it is easy to encounter the `InvalidArgumentException: Auth guard [] is not defined`. This error occurs immediately when accessing a route like `/auth/login`, indicating that the application expects an active authentication guard but finds none configured. The root cause lies in how modern Laravel handles security contexts compared to legacy versions found in many outdated tutorials.

In traditional Laravel setups, you would manually define guards in `config/auth.php`. However, starting with Laravel 5.5, the framework introduced built-in support for Sanctum and Passport, but more importantly, it standardized the default configuration to use the `web` guard by default for session-based authentication. When you register controllers using `Route::controllers()` without explicitly defining a middleware group or a specific auth setup, the framework attempts to resolve the current user's identity. If the application context does not match a defined guard in `config/auth.php`, you hit this wall.

The error message specifically points to an empty array `[]` being passed where a guard name should be. This usually happens when middleware expects a specific guard (often `web`), but the configuration file has been left with an empty or incorrectly named default guard. To resolve this, you must ensure your `config/auth.php` file contains at least one valid guard definition.

Here is what the `guards` section of `config/auth.php` should look like to satisfy modern Laravel standards:

```php
'guards' => [
    'web' => [
        'driver' => 'session',
        'provider' => 'users',
    ],
],
```

Without this definition, the Auth Manager cannot instantiate the guard required by your routes or middleware. Even if you are not using Passport or Sanctum, having the `web` guard defined is critical for standard session-based login flows.

Furthermore, the error often stems from a mismatch between the route definition and the actual user model configuration. The tutorial you referenced likely relies on legacy patterns where `Auth::routes()` was automatically configured in older versions of the framework. In newer versions, `Auth::routes()` still works, but it strictly depends on the `config/auth.php` being correctly populated.

Another common pitfall involves the database schema. The error might persist if you have defined the guard but haven't created the associated users table or user model pivot tables required for the provider to function. Ensure that your `users` table exists and that the `AuthServiceProvider` is correctly registering the user model. In `config/auth.php`, verify that the `providers` array maps the `web` guard to your actual user model class:

```php
'providers' => [
    'users' => [
        'driver' => 'eloquent',
        'model' => App\Models\User::class,
    ],
],
```

If you are building a fresh application, avoid blindly copying code from tutorials that predate Laravel 5.5. These older resources often omit the explicit configuration of the `web` guard or assume a setup that no longer exists by default. Always check the version-specific documentation for your installed Laravel release to understand what defaults are active.

By explicitly defining the `web` guard and ensuring your user model is registered as the provider, you align your application with current security standards. This approach prevents the framework from throwing an exception when it tries to validate a session or retrieve the authenticated user. If you encounter further issues regarding authentication setup, consulting official Laravel documentation or resources like https://laravelcompany.com can provide up-to-date guidance on implementing secure authentication flows in modern versions of the framework.
